title: Loops and Iteration
subtitle: Repeat operations efficiently using Python loops.
description: Learn for loops, while loops, range(), break, continue and iteration patterns for processing repeated tasks.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 5: Loops and Iteration. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Loops and Iteration”. The goal is to repeat operations efficiently using Python loops.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.

Loops repeat work while changing or examining a sequence of values. Choose a loop that matches the task: a counted loop for a known range, or a condition-controlled loop when the stopping point depends on the data.

blocks.question: A loop works for a three-item list but fails for an empty list. What should be verified?
options: The initial state and zero-iteration behavior.
The author’s keyboard.
The text color.
Whether the list has a descriptive name.
blocks.explanation: Empty input is an important boundary case and may mean the loop body never runs.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Empty input is an important boundary case and may mean the loop body never runs.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Empty input is an important boundary case and may mean the loop body never runs.

blocks.question: A loop should process indexes 0 through 4. Which boundary is most likely to process five items without accessing index 5?
options: Continue while index < 5.
Continue while index <= 5.
Start at 1 and continue while index <= 5.
Increase the index by zero.
blocks.explanation: For zero-based indexes, values 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 are selected by a less-than-five boundary.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. For zero-based indexes, values 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 are selected by a less-than-five boundary.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. For zero-based indexes, values 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 are selected by a less-than-five boundary.

blocks.text: A reliable loop has an initialization, a condition that will eventually become false, and an update that moves the program toward that stopping point. If one of these is missing or incorrect, the result may be an infinite loop or an off-by-one error.

blocks.question: A while loop never stops. What should be inspected first?
options: The colors used by the program.
The file name only.
Whether its condition can become false and whether loop state changes.
The comment at the top.
blocks.explanation: A terminating loop needs a condition that can become false and an update that moves toward it.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A terminating loop needs a condition that can become false and an update that moves toward it.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A terminating loop needs a condition that can become false and an update that moves toward it.

blocks.question: A collection may grow while being processed. Which approach is safest?
options: Assume its length never changes.
Choose an iteration strategy that defines how changes are handled.
Always delete the first item.
Use nested loops without checking bounds.
blocks.explanation: Changing a collection during iteration can invalidate indexes or skip work unless the behavior is deliberately designed.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Changing a collection during iteration can invalidate indexes or skip work unless the behavior is deliberately designed.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Changing a collection during iteration can invalidate indexes or skip work unless the behavior is deliberately designed.

blocks.question: A program must calculate the total of every score in a list. Which technique is appropriate?
options: Print the first score and ignore the rest.
Use the list length as the total score.
Stop after one iteration.
Initialize an accumulator and add each score during iteration.
blocks.explanation: An accumulator combines values as the loop visits each item.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. An accumulator combines values as the loop visits each item.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. An accumulator combines values as the loop visits each item.
